Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# bootstrap-home.sh [--root DIR] [options]
3	#
4	# Give one checkout — a repo root or a worktree — its own Skill Manager home,
5	# so every agent launched from it reads and writes that home instead of the
6	# operator's global one.
7	#
8	# This is the ONLY implementation of that sequence. `new-change.sh` calls it
9	# for every worktree it creates, and a repo's own `scripts/agent-home.sh`
10	# locates and calls this same file. There is deliberately no second copy of
11	# the ordering rules: getting them wrong writes into the operator's home,
12	# which is the one failure this script exists to make impossible.
13	#
14	# The order is not cosmetic
15	# ------------------------
16	#   clone  ->  point SKILL_MANAGER_HOME at the clone  ->  everything else
17	#
18	# `project resolve`, `sync`, `install`, `bind` and friends all write into
19	# whatever `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` names (`SkillStore.defaultStore()`), and
20	# `project resolve` additionally writes a child-home record and a binding
21	# ledger into that store. Run any of them before the clone exists and they
22	# land in the global home. So: `skill-manager home clone` is the first
23	# command, it is the only command that names the source home, and every
24	# command after it runs with SKILL_MANAGER_HOME exported to the clone.
25	# `require_local_home` re-asserts that before any mutating step, so the rule
26	# is enforced by the script rather than remembered by a caller.
27	#
28	# What it produces under <root>:
29	#   .skill-manager/                     the home (a clone of the source home)
30	#   .skill-manager/home.runtime.json    the launch descriptor (HomeDescriptor)
31	#   .skill-manager/home.policy.toml     live | frozen (HomePolicy)
32	#   .skill-manager/bin/launch/{claude,codex,gemini}   launcher shims
33	#   .claude/ .codex/ .gemini/           agent homes, at the paths the
34	#                                       descriptor's env block names
35	#
36	# Add those to the PARENT repo's root .gitignore, never to a file inside a
37	# constituent (INTEGRATION.md rule 2).
38	SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"; . "$SCRIPT_DIR/lib.sh"
39	
40	usage() {
41	  cat >&2 <<'EOF'
42	usage: bootstrap-home.sh [DIR | --root DIR] [--source HOME] [--policy live|frozen]
43	                         [--print-env] [--force] [--quiet] [--verbose]
44	                         [--onboard [--onboard-gateway]] [--allow-empty]
45	
46	  DIR              Checkout to give a home to, positionally -- the same thing
47	                   --root names. Accepted because every other front door in
48	                   this pair takes its subject that way.
49	  --root DIR       Checkout to give a home to. Default: the nearest enclosing
50	                   git toplevel — which inside a constituent is the
51	                   CONSTITUENT, not the integration repo tracking its files.
52	  --source HOME    Home to clone from. Only ever read. Default: for a LINKED
53	                   WORKTREE, its project home (the main working tree's), which
54	                   is the home close-change.sh reconciles it back into; for a
55	                   main working tree, $SKILL_MANAGER_HOME, else ~/.skill-manager.
56	                   A --source that disagrees with a worktree's project home is
57	                   REFUSED, not silently honoured.
58	  --policy P       Policy to declare on the new home: live (default) or
59	                   frozen. A home that is ALREADY frozen is never touched.
60	  --print-env      Print the launch environment as `export` lines and exit.
61	                   Bootstraps first if needed. Safe to `eval`.
62	  --force          Re-run the steps on an existing live home. Never applies
63	                   to a frozen one, and never re-clones over an existing
64	                   store.
65	  --quiet          Say nothing at all on a successful run. The log is still
66	                   written; failures are still reported.
67	  --verbose        Put the whole log on stderr as it happens, instead of the
68	                   five-line summary. Nothing is withheld either way — a quiet
69	                   run names the log file that holds all of it.
70	  --onboard        When the finished home has NO skills, run
71	                   `skill-manager onboard --skip-gateway` on it instead of
72	                   refusing. Only legal for a MAIN working tree: onboarding a
73	                   WORKTREE home would give it units its project home never had,
74	                   and every one of those blocks teardown (issue #50).
75	  --onboard-gateway  With --onboard, also start the gateway. Off by default
76	                   because the gateway is a contended singleton
77	                   (skill-manager#132) and a bootstrap is not the place to
78	                   contend for it.
79	  --allow-empty    Accept a home with zero skills. Downgrades the refusal to a
80	                   warning; the home is still reported as EMPTY, never as
81	                   verified.
82	  --no-project     Do not run the `sync --skip-mcp` that projects this home's
83	                   skills into its agent homes. The home will hold skills that
84	                   no agent launched here can read; combine with
85	                   --allow-unprojected or the run refuses.
86	  --allow-unprojected  Accept a home whose skills are not reachable from its
87	                   agent homes. Downgrades the refusal to a warning; the home is
88	                   never reported as verified.
89	
90	On success stderr carries five lines and nothing else: home, projected,
91	verified, launch, log. On failure it carries a bounded tail of the log and the
92	log's path. Stdout is reserved for --print-env.
93	
94	Exit codes: 0 ok - 1 usage/setup error - 5 the home has no skills
95	            6 the home's skills are not projected into its agent homes
96	EOF
97	}
98	
99	# A home with zero skills is a distinct outcome from a broken one, and callers
100	# (new-change.sh, `wt`) route it to a different remedy, so it gets its own code.
101	EMPTY_EXIT=5
102	# And a home that HOLDS skills no agent can read is a third outcome, with a
103	# third remedy. It used to be reported as `verified`.
104	UNPROJECTED_EXIT=6
105	
106	ROOT=""; SOURCE=""; POLICY="live"; PRINT_ENV=0; FORCE=0; QUIET=0; VERBOSE=0
107	ONBOARD=0; ONBOARD_GATEWAY=0; ALLOW_EMPTY=0; NO_PROJECT=0; ALLOW_UNPROJECTED=0
108	# Set when `--onboard`'s install step exits non-zero. It is a fact about what
109	# this home HOLDS, so it survives to the closing banner rather than being turned
110	# into an exit code on the spot — the gates below own the codes.
111	ONBOARD_SHORTFALL=0
112	ROOT_POSITIONAL=""
113	while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
114	  case "$1" in
115	    --root)      ROOT="${2:?--root needs a directory}"; shift 2 ;;
116	    --source)    SOURCE="${2:?--source needs a directory}"; shift 2 ;;
117	    --policy)    POLICY="${2:?--policy needs live|frozen}"; shift 2 ;;
118	    --print-env) PRINT_ENV=1; shift ;;
119	    --force)     FORCE=1; shift ;;
120	    --quiet)     QUIET=1; shift ;;
121	    --verbose|-v) VERBOSE=1; shift ;;
122	    --onboard)   ONBOARD=1; shift ;;
123	    --onboard-gateway) ONBOARD=1; ONBOARD_GATEWAY=1; shift ;;
124	    --allow-empty) ALLOW_EMPTY=1; shift ;;
125	    --no-project)  NO_PROJECT=1; shift ;;
126	    --allow-unprojected) ALLOW_UNPROJECTED=1; shift ;;
127	    -h|--help)   usage; exit 0 ;;
128	    # A BARE DIRECTORY IS THE ROOT. Measured in the home-bootstrap eval: an
129	    # agent that had found this script and read its usage still wrote
130	    #
131	    #     bootstrap-home.sh /path/to/checkout
132	    #
133	    # and got `unknown argument`. The second front door in this pair --
134	    # `wt new <ticket> <base>` -- takes its subject positionally, and so does

163	#   used to be printed is in it, in order, including every byte the CLI wrote.

170	#

174	# The mechanism is one redirection rather than a rewrite of every call site: fd 2
175	# becomes the log, so every existing `>&2` — this script's prose, its refusals,
176	# and the output of every CLI child it runs — lands there without a second

183	# concurrent bootstraps would interleave into it. Measured here, on the first

193	  # the console carries ONE stream in ONE order and there is nothing to interleave.

215	# transcript, which is exactly the material this change exists to stop printing.

227	# The log line comes FIRST here and last on a successful run, and that is not an
228	# inconsistency. `wt` answers a child that died without emitting a contract by
229	# quoting its last `error:` line as the FAILED reason, and where there is none —
230	# a bare `set -e` failure, a git command's own message — THE LAST NON-EMPTY LINE
231	# OF ITS STDERR. Either way a failure whose last line is a file path would hand
232	# the caller a path where the reason should be. The failure's own last line has
233	# to stay last.
234	report_failure() {
235	  local total
236	  total="$(command wc -l < "$LOG" 2>/dev/null | command tr -d ' ')" || total=0

238	  if [ "$total" -gt "$LOG_TAIL" ]; then
239	    printf 'log:       %s  (%s earlier line(s) omitted below)\n' "$LOG" "$((total - LOG_TAIL))" >&3
240	  else
241	    printf 'log:       %s\n' "$LOG" >&3
242	  fi

316	# is not that it is tidier:

320	#     refuses either way. To be the mechanism it would have to be COMMITTED,
321	#     which is a far larger authority than "create a directory": it lands on
322	#     whatever branch happens to be checked out, has no quiet undo, and would

324	#     REFUSING until someone commits the rules — was implemented and measured,

339	# discovered: THIS RULE IS INVISIBLE TO EVERY OTHER CLONE. It makes the checkout

348	# Top-level untracked entries, one per line, directories with a trailing slash.

407	# Write an exclude rule for every top-level entry this run created and left
408	# untracked, and for every untracked entry the home machinery owns by name.
409	# Idempotent, and silent when there is nothing to add.
410	#
411	# Two rules, not one, because they cover different runs. The first catches
412	# whatever THIS run produced, whatever it is called — including a file no rule
413	# anticipates. The second catches what an earlier `install` / `sync` /
414	# `project resolve` left behind, which the first cannot see: on a re-run those
415	# files are already untracked before this script starts, so "new since the
416	# snapshot" is empty and the tree stays dirty. The documented onboarding
417	# sequence is bootstrap-then-install, so that re-run IS the ordinary case.

422	# do not race.

434	    [ -n "$entry" ] || continue
435	    if printf '%s\n' "$UNTRACKED_BEFORE" | command grep -qxF "$entry"; then
436	      # Not new. Ignore it only if the home machinery owns the name; anything
437	      # else the operator already had untracked is theirs, and silently
438	      # excluding it would hide their own work.
439	      home_owns_name "$entry" "$owned" || continue
440	    fi
441	    rule="/$entry"
442	    [ -f "$excl" ] && command grep -qxF "$rule" "$excl" && continue
443	    mkdir -p "$common/info"
444	    if [ "$added" = 0 ]; then
445	      printf '\n# git-integration-repo bootstrap-home.sh: per-checkout Skill Manager\n# home artefacts, created at %s. Local to this clone; the shared rules\n# belong in .gitignore (references/skill-homes.md).\n' \
446	        "$ROOT" >> "$excl"
447	      added=1
448	    fi
449	    printf '%s\n' "$rule" >> "$excl"
450	    say "ignored:   $rule -> $excl"
451	  done <<EOF
452	$after
453	EOF

583	  other command writes a home that is not the global one.)
584	  Or copy a home that already exists somewhere else:
585	    $SCRIPT_DIR/bootstrap-home.sh --root '$ROOT' --source '<an existing home>'" ;;
586	  esac
587	fi
588	SOURCE="$(cd "$SOURCE" && pwd -P)"

590	# The agreement, asserted. Only reachable via an explicit --source, since the
591	# defaults above make the two equal by construction — which is the point: this
592	# turns the one remaining way to disagree into a refusal instead of a worktree
593	# that cannot be closed.
594	if [ "$IS_WORKTREE" = 1 ] && [ -n "$PROJECT_HOME" ] && [ "$SOURCE" != "$PROJECT_HOME" ]; then
595	  die "refusing to clone this worktree's home from a home it cannot be closed into.
596	    source (--source):  $SOURCE
597	    close-out --into:   $PROJECT_HOME
598	  close-change.sh reconciles <worktree>/.skill-manager INTO the project home, so
599	  a home cloned from anywhere else arrives holding units that home never had —
600	  every one of them a blocker at teardown (issue #50). Drop --source to use the
601	  project home, or bootstrap the project home from $SOURCE first so the two
602	  agree."
603	fi
604	
605	# The guard. A bootstrap that can target the operator's own home is not a
606	# bootstrap, it is the bug — so the refusals come before anything is read,
607	# written, or exported.
608	[ "$ROOT" = "$HOME" ]          && die "refusing to bootstrap \$HOME as a project checkout ($ROOT)"
609	[ "$STORE" = "$GLOBAL_HOME" ]  && die "refusing to write the global home at $GLOBAL_HOME"
610	[ "$STORE" = "$SOURCE" ]       && die "refusing to bootstrap a home from itself ($STORE)"
611	
612	# Every mutating step goes through this, so "point SKILL_MANAGER_HOME at the
613	# clone first" is a property of the script and not of the caller's memory.
614	require_local_home() {
615	  local what="$1"
616	  [ "${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-}" = "$STORE" ] \
617	    || die "$what: SKILL_MANAGER_HOME is '${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-unset}', not the local home $STORE"
618	  [ "$SKILL_MANAGER_HOME" != "$GLOBAL_HOME" ] \
619	    || die "$what: SKILL_MANAGER_HOME resolves to the global home"
620	  [ -d "$STORE" ] || die "$what: local home $STORE does not exist yet"

623	# -------------------------------------------------------------------- CLI
624	
625	# Which skill-manager runs this. Same first rule as
626	# HomeDescriptor.resolveCli — an explicit SKILL_MANAGER_CLI pin wins.
627	#
628	# The capability probe exists because `home` is newer than the released CLI:
629	# without it a stale skill-manager is picked and fails deep inside the
630	# sequence, after directories have already been created.
631	#
632	# The probe reads the help TEXT rather than the exit status alone, and that is
633	# still deliberate: the released 0.19.2 answers an unknown subcommand by
634	# printing top-level usage and exiting 0 (newer builds exit 2), so a
635	# status-only probe accepts a CLI with no `home` command at all.
636	#
637	# HBR-2: IT READ THE TEXT *INSTEAD OF* THE STATUS, AND THREW THE STATUS AWAY.
638	# The probe was one line:
639	#
640	#   cli_has_home() { "$1" home clone --help 2>&1 | grep -q -- '--to'; }
641	#
642	# In a pipeline the function's status is GREP's, so the candidate's own exit
643	# code never survived — 0, 2, 79 and 127 all arrived as "no `--to`", and the
644	# sole discriminator left was whether a string appeared. So every way of
645	# failing rendered as the same sentence:
646	#
647	#   on PATH: <other home>/bin/cli/skill-manager (too old — `home clone` is missing)
648	#
649	# about a CLI that was not old and does have `home clone`. It is another home's
650	# ENTRYPOINT, and it refused because SKILL_MANAGER_HOME named a third home —
651	# `pick_cli` runs before this script exports SKILL_MANAGER_HOME, so the probe
652	# runs under the CALLER's ambient home, which is the trigger. The signal was
653	# already there and already unique: the shim exits 79
654	# (LauncherShims.HOME_MISMATCH_EXIT_CODE), chosen so a caller could tell a
655	# refusal from the self-exec refusal at 78, and it collides with nothing this
656	# script sees. It was emitted and discarded.
657	#
658	# So the probe now returns a VERDICT and no pipeline hides the status.
659	CLI_HOME_MISMATCH_EXIT=79   # LauncherShims.HOME_MISMATCH_EXIT_CODE
660	
661	# The home a candidate BINDS, or empty when it is not a home entrypoint.
662	#
663	# Structural, not textual, and it runs NOTHING. A generated entrypoint lives at
664	# <home>/bin/cli/skill-manager and derives its home as `../..` — so this reads
665	# the same two levels the shim itself reads and cannot drift from it. Deriving
666	# it instead of grepping for a marker also catches the pre-#61 PATH-searching
667	# shims, which carry no marker at all (see PATH_SHIM_MARKER below).
668	#
669	# WHY A TEXT TEST WHEN EXIT 79 IS RIGHT THERE: because the two fixes for this
670	# defect ship on opposite sides of a version skew. A CLI old enough to predate
671	# the refusal, or new enough to have been taught that `--help` names no home
672	# and so to answer it, both return 0 here — and neither is usable to bootstrap
673	# a DIFFERENT home while SKILL_MANAGER_HOME names a third one. This clause and
674	# the exit-code clause below cover each other; whichever build is installed,
675	# the refusal is named as a refusal.
676	cli_binds_home() {
677	  local cli="$1" dir home
678	  case "$cli" in */bin/cli/skill-manager) ;; *) return 0 ;; esac
679	  dir="$(cd "$(dirname "$cli")" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)" || return 0
680	  home="$(cd "$dir/../.." 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)" || return 0
681	  if [ -f "$home/home.runtime.json" ] \
682	     || { [ -d "$home/installed" ] && [ -d "$home/skills" ]; }; then
683	    printf '%s\n' "$home"
684	  fi
685	}
686	
687	# Where the last probe's own words are kept. cli_verdict runs inside a command
688	# substitution, so a shell variable would die with the subshell; a file does
689	# not. The point is that the candidate's OWN diagnostic reaches the report —
690	# summarising a failure into one adjective is how this defect started.
691	CLI_PROBE_OUT="$_LOG_TMP.probe"
692	
693	# ok | refused | old | broken — the four things a candidate can be, kept apart.
694	# Printed rather than returned as a status so `set -e` cannot swallow it and so
695	# the caller can put the word straight into a diagnostic.
696	#
697	# `broken` is here because `old` was silently the catch-all, and that is the
698	# same defect one level down. Measured while fixing this: a home entrypoint
699	# probed with a PATH that did not carry `jbang` could not start its JVM at all,
700	# exited 127, printed no `--to`, and was reported as a build that "predates
701	# `home clone`". Nothing was old. Anything that is not a real answer about the
702	# command surface must not be scored as one.
703	cli_verdict() {
704	  local cli="$1" status=0 bound named
705	  : > "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" 2>/dev/null || true
706	
707	  # THE PROBE RUNS FIRST, ALWAYS, AND ITS BYTES ARE ALWAYS KEPT — including on
708	  # the paths that are about to be decided without them. The old probe piped
709	  # into `grep -q`, which threw away the candidate's exit code AND everything
710	  # it said; skt (HBR-3) then relayed bootstrap's "too old" faithfully, because
711	  # the shim's own words had never reached it. Correcting only the status would
712	  # leave the reader with a bare verdict and no evidence, so `> "$CLI_PROBE_OUT"
713	  # 2>&1` replaces the pipe: same redirection, but the text survives and so does
714	  # `$?`.
715	  "$cli" home clone --help > "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" 2>&1 || status=$?
716	
717	  [ "$status" = "$CLI_HOME_MISMATCH_EXIT" ] && { printf 'refused\n'; return 0; }
718	  [ "$status" = 127 ] && { printf 'broken\n'; return 0; }
719	
720	  # The structural clause, for the other side of the version skew: a build new
721	  # enough to answer a help request truthfully returns 0 here and says nothing
722	  # about homes, so there is no refusal text to relay — because there was no
723	  # refusal. The report line names both homes itself in that case, which is what
724	  # the shim's own message would have said.
725	  bound="$(cli_binds_home "$cli")"
726	  named="${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-}"
727	  [ -n "$named" ] && named="$(cd "$named" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P || printf '%s' "$named")"
728	  if [ -n "$bound" ] && [ -n "$named" ] && [ "$bound" != "$named" ]; then
729	    # The candidate answered the help request rather than refusing it, so what
730	    # it said is a usage screen and not a refusal. Drop it: relaying it under
731	    # "It said:" would present help text as if it were the explanation.
732	    : > "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" 2>/dev/null || true
733	    printf 'refused\n'; return 0
734	  fi
735	
736	  if command grep -q -- '--to' "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" 2>/dev/null; then
737	    printf 'ok\n'
738	  else
739	    printf 'old\n'
740	  fi
741	}
742	
743	# One line of the failure report, so (a) a refusal, (b) a genuinely old build
744	# and (c) nothing at all cannot render as the same sentence again.
745	cli_verdict_line() {
746	  local verdict="$1" cli="$2" bound
747	  case "$verdict" in
748	    refused)
749	      bound="$(cli_binds_home "$cli")"
750	      printf '    refused: %s\n' "$cli"
751	      printf '             it is the entrypoint of the home %s, which binds that\n' \
752	        "${bound:-it lives in}"
753	      printf '             home and will not act on another. SKILL_MANAGER_HOME names\n'
754	      printf '             %s. NOTHING IS OUT OF DATE.\n' "${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-<unset>}"
755	      # AND ITS OWN WORDS, when it had any. A build that refuses says which two
756	      # homes are in play and how to name one; that sentence is the useful half
757	      # of this report and the old probe deleted it. Empty only when the
758	      # candidate did not refuse in words — see the structural clause above.
759	      if [ -s "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" ]; then
760	        printf '             It said:\n'
761	        cli_probe_said
762	      fi
763	      ;;
764	    old)
765	      printf '    too old: %s\n' "$cli"
766	      printf '             it answered `home clone --help` without a `--to`, so this\n'
767	      printf '             build predates `home clone`. It said:\n'
768	      cli_probe_said
769	      ;;
770	    broken)
771	      printf '    broken:  %s\n' "$cli"
772	      printf '             it exited 127, so it could not run at all — a missing\n'
773	      printf '             interpreter or a pin naming a build that is gone. This is\n'
774	      printf '             not a version problem. It said:\n'
775	      cli_probe_said
776	      ;;
777	  esac
778	}
779	
780	# The candidate's own words, indented and bounded. Bounded because a usage dump
781	# is long; present at all because "too old" was, for every one of these cases,
782	# the only thing the operator was ever told.
783	cli_probe_said() {
784	  [ -s "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" ] || { printf '               (nothing)\n'; return 0; }
785	  # Six lines reaches "this shim would have edited: <home>" in a refusal, which
786	  # is the line the reader needs, without dumping a whole usage screen.
787	  sed -n '1,6p' "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" | sed 's/^/               /'
788	}
789	
790	pick_cli() {
791	  local pinned="${SKILL_MANAGER_CLI:-}" verdict report="" c
792	  if [ -n "$pinned" ]; then
793	    [ -x "$pinned" ] || die "SKILL_MANAGER_CLI is not executable: $pinned"
794	    verdict="$(cli_verdict "$pinned")"
795	    [ "$verdict" = ok ] || die "SKILL_MANAGER_CLI cannot bootstrap this home.
796	$(cli_verdict_line "$verdict" "$pinned")
797	  Point SKILL_MANAGER_CLI at a skill-manager BUILD rather than at a home's
798	  entrypoint, or unset SKILL_MANAGER_HOME so nothing is being aimed elsewhere."
799	    printf '%s\n' "$pinned"; return 0
800	  fi
801	
802	  # A CLI the checkout itself ships, then one the enclosing INTEGRATION repo
803	  # ships. The second entry is what lets a constituent home find a capable
804	  # build: bootstrapping constituents/deploy-helm searched only deploy-helm,
805	  # which ships no skill-manager, so it died — or, worse, the caller exported
806	  # SKILL_MANAGER_CLI once by hand and the pin was never recorded anywhere.
807	  # The integration parent is where the epic build actually lives.
808	  #
809	  # HBR-2 PUT PATH LAST, and reversed an ordering this comment used to argue
810	  # for. The old order tried PATH before the checkout's own build, because a
811	  # checkout's copy can be older than the installed release. That reason is now
812	  # served by the verdict instead: an `old` candidate is skipped and PATH is
813	  # still reached, so nothing is lost — while PATH-FIRST cost something real.
814	  # On a machine that bootstraps worktree homes, the `skill-manager` on PATH is
815	  # very often some OTHER home's bin/cli entrypoint, and preferring it is how a
816	  # bootstrap ends up asking the one CLI that is guaranteed to refuse. A build
817	  # is a better answer to "which skill-manager runs this" than a shim bound to
818	  # a home that is not the one being built.
819	  local candidate integration seen=""
820	  integration="$(outermost_integration_root "$ROOT")"
821	  c="$(command -v skill-manager || true)"
822	  for candidate in "$ROOT/skill-manager" "$ROOT"/constituents/*/skill-manager \
823	                   ${integration:+"$integration/skill-manager" "$integration"/constituents/*/skill-manager} \
824	                   ${c:+"$c"}; do
825	    [ -x "$candidate" ] || continue
826	    [ -d "$candidate" ] && continue
827	    # One entry can appear twice — the PATH `skill-manager` IS this checkout's
828	    # own build whenever the operator put it there, and the integration parent
829	    # of a constituent is reached by two of the globs. Probing it twice costs a
830	    # second JVM start and reports the same candidate under two bullets, which
831	    # reads as two problems.
832	    case " $seen " in *" $candidate "*) continue ;; esac
833	    seen="$seen $candidate"
834	    verdict="$(cli_verdict "$candidate")"
835	    [ "$verdict" = ok ] && { printf '%s\n' "$candidate"; return 0; }
836	    report="$report$(cli_verdict_line "$verdict" "$candidate")
837	"
838	  done
839	
840	  # (c) — nothing was even a candidate. Said as its own sentence, because the
841	  # message this replaces recommended "install a newer skill-manager" here too,
842	  # which names a version problem where there is no skill-manager to have a
843	  # version.
844	  [ -n "$report" ] || die "no skill-manager CLI was found at all.
845	    nothing named \`skill-manager\` is on PATH, and neither $ROOT nor any
846	    enclosing integration repo ships one.
847	  Install skill-manager, or set SKILL_MANAGER_CLI to a build.
848	  Without it a worktree cannot get its own home, and an agent would run
849	  against the operator's global home."
850	
851	  die "no skill-manager CLI that can bootstrap a home was usable. Every candidate,
852	  and why each one was not it:
853	$report  Set SKILL_MANAGER_CLI to a build that can, and if a candidate above was
854	  REFUSED rather than old, unset SKILL_MANAGER_HOME first — a refusal is about
855	  which home you aimed at, not about the CLI's version, and upgrading will not
856	  change it.
857	  Without one a worktree cannot get its own home, and an agent would run
858	  against the operator's global home."
859	}
860	
861	CLI="$(pick_cli)"
862	
863	# --------------------------------------------------------------- policy read
864	
865	# HomePolicy is the predicate — asking the CLI keeps this script from becoming
866	# a second parser of home.policy.toml.
867	home_policy() { "$CLI" home policy --home "$STORE" 2>/dev/null | awk '/^policy:/ {print $2}'; }
868	
869	# The agent-home directories this home declares. Read from the descriptor
870	# (HomeDescriptor.envFor) rather than hardcoded here, so this script cannot
871	# create `.claude` in a place the launcher will not look.
872	#
873	# ASKED ONCE PER RUN, and that is the single largest saving this script has ever
874	# made. Measured on a `wt new` against an 18-unit / 852 MB home, before this
875	# cache: 151.7 s wall clock, of which ~100 s was this function.
876	#
877	# It is a JVM start (~1.4 s), and it was called from inside PER-UNIT LOOPS.
878	# `unprojected_pairs` and `projected_unit_count` both iterate the store's units
879	# and, for each one, expand `$(projection_dirs)` — a command substitution, so a
880	# fresh subshell, so a fresh JVM — 18 units x 1.4 s = 25 s per call, and there
881	# are four such calls in a bootstrap (the projection guard, the re-check after
882	# materializing, and both counters in verify()). Nothing about the answer varies
883	# across them: it is a pure function of $STORE and $ROOT, neither of which
884	# changes after the clone.
885	#
886	# A memo assigned INSIDE the function would not have helped, and that is the
887	# whole reason this is shaped as an explicit prime: the assignment would happen
888	# in the `$( )` subshell and be discarded with it, so every iteration would miss
889	# the cache. `prime_env_dirs` is therefore called from TOP-LEVEL statements only,
890	# where the assignment survives.
891	#
892	# Empty is never cached: an empty answer means the descriptor could not be read
893	# (the `2>/dev/null` swallows why), and caching that would turn a transient
894	# failure into a permanent one for the rest of the run.
895	ENV_DIRS_CACHE=""
896	_descriptor_env_dirs_uncached() {
897	  "$CLI" home describe --home "$STORE" --home-root "$ROOT" --json 2>/dev/null | "$PY" -c '
898	import json, sys
899	try:
900	    d = json.load(sys.stdin)
901	except Exception:
902	    sys.exit(0)
903	env = d.get("env") or {}
904	for key in ("CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR", "CODEX_HOME", "GEMINI_HOME"):
905	    value = env.get(key)
906	    if value:
907	        print(value)
908	'
909	}
910	prime_env_dirs() {
911	  [ -z "$ENV_DIRS_CACHE" ] || return 0
912	  ENV_DIRS_CACHE="$(_descriptor_env_dirs_uncached)"
913	  return 0
914	}
915	descriptor_env_dirs() {
916	  if [ -n "$ENV_DIRS_CACHE" ]; then printf '%s\n' "$ENV_DIRS_CACHE"; return 0; fi
917	  _descriptor_env_dirs_uncached
918	}
919	
920	# The agent-home env as `NAME=VALUE` words, ready to hand to `env`. Any command
921	# that writes agent bindings — `sync` above all — must run with these set, or it
922	# writes the OPERATOR'S ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex/config.toml and
923	# ~/.gemini/settings.json instead of this home's. Measured: `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME=<home>
924	# skill-manager sync --force-scripts`, the remedy this script used to print
925	# verbatim, reported `ADDED claude (~/.claude.json)` — the global-binding hijack
926	# recorded as skill-manager#145, printed as an instruction by THIS file. Naming
927	# the home is not enough; the agent-home variables are a separate axis.
928	agent_env_words() {
929	  local dir
930	  descriptor_env_dirs | while IFS= read -r dir; do
931	    [ -n "$dir" ] || continue
932	    case "$dir" in
933	      */.claude) printf 'CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=%s\n' "$dir" ;;
934	      */.codex)  printf 'CODEX_HOME=%s\n' "$dir" ;;
935	      */.gemini) printf 'GEMINI_HOME=%s\n' "$dir" ;;
936	    esac
937	  done
938	}
939	
940	# A shell-quoted `env ...` prefix that pins BOTH axes. This is the only spelling
941	# of a home-mutating command this script is allowed to print.
942	home_env_prefix() {
943	  local out="env SKILL_MANAGER_HOME=$STORE" word
944	  while IFS= read -r word; do [ -n "$word" ] && out="$out ${word%%=*}=${word#*=}"; done <<EOF
945	$(agent_env_words)
946	EOF
947	  printf '%s\n' "$out"
948	}
949	
950	# How many skills this home can actually serve. Directories only, and only ones
951	# carrying a SKILL.md, so a stray file or an empty leftover directory cannot
952	# make an empty home look populated — which is the whole point of the count.
953	home_skill_count() { skill_count "$STORE"; }
954	skill_count() {
955	  local d n=0
956	  for d in "$1"/skills/*/; do
957	    [ -d "$d" ] || continue
958	    [ -f "$d/SKILL.md" ] || continue
959	    n=$((n + 1))
960	  done
961	  printf '%s\n' "$n"
962	}
963	
964	# Symlinks inside the home that do not resolve. `skill-manager home verify`
965	# refuses a home over exactly these, which is how bootstrap came to report
966	# `verified` on a home `home verify` rejects. Found here with `find` rather than
967	# with a second CLI start: it is the same fact, it costs no JVM, and it is still
968	# answerable on the --force path where no clone report exists.
969	#
970	# RE-MEASURED 2026-08-23, AND THE TRIGGER CHANGED WHILE THE CONSEQUENCE DID NOT.
971	# This comment used to say `home clone` skips venvs/, tools/, npm/ and cache/,
972	# "so any link INTO one of them arrives dangling". That is no longer true. A
973	# lazy clone (`lazy_artifacts = true`, the default for a project or worktree

975	# exits 86 naming `skill-manager build <id>` -- not a symlink. `find -type l`
976	# with `! -e` therefore finds NOTHING on a healthy lazy clone, and this function
977	# correctly returns empty there.
978	#
979	# What it still finds, and what `home verify` still refuses over, is a link that
980	# genuinely does not resolve. Measured both ways on one home: clean lazy clone
981	# -> "every reference ... resolves", exit 0; the same home plus one planted
982	# `bin/cli/fixture-dangling -> ../../venvs/fixture-missing/bin/tool` -> "1
983	# reference(s) ... do not resolve", exit 1. So the report below is not stale --
984	# its PREMISE was. The contract this sits inside is stated once, in
985	# ${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/plugins/skt/skills/skt/references/derived-artifacts.md
986	# (absent in a home without skt).
987	dangling_home_links() {
988	  command find "$STORE/bin" -type l 2>/dev/null | while IFS= read -r link; do
989	    [ -e "$link" ] || printf '%s -> %s\n' "${link#"$STORE"/}" "$(readlink "$link")"
990	  done
991	}
992	
993	# ------------------------------------------------------------- the CLI pin
994	#
995	# <home>/bin/cli/skill-manager decides which build every launch from this home
996	# runs: the generated launchers read it, and HomeDescriptor.resolveCli
997	# documents it as rule 3. Since issue #61 the launchers have NO PATH fallback
998	# at all, so a wrong or missing pin is not a downgrade, it is a home that
999	# cannot launch.
1000	#
1001	# THIS SCRIPT NO LONGER WRITES THAT FILE.
1002	#
1003	# It used to, and it was right to: `skill-manager home shims` wrote a
1004	# PATH-RESOLVING shim, and PATH's skill-manager on this machine is the released
1005	# 0.19.2 — which has no `exec` subcommand, so every generated launcher ended in
1006	# `Unmatched arguments: 'exec'`. Homes bootstrapped through this script worked
1007	# and homes provisioned by `home shims` alone did not, and because this script
1008	# masked the difference for the whole 24-repo onboarding fan-out, nobody saw
1009	# it.
1010	#
1011	# skill-manager fixed it (issue #61, commit e65962e): `home shims` now writes
1012	# the absolute pin itself, derived from the build that is running it

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# bootstrap-home.sh [--root DIR] [options]
#
# Give one checkout — a repo root or a worktree — its own Skill Manager home,
# so every agent launched from it reads and writes that home instead of the
# operator's global one.
#
# This is the ONLY implementation of that sequence. `new-change.sh` calls it
# for every worktree it creates, and a repo's own `scripts/agent-home.sh`
# locates and calls this same file. There is deliberately no second copy of
# the ordering rules: getting them wrong writes into the operator's home,
# which is the one failure this script exists to make impossible.
#
# The order is not cosmetic
# ------------------------
#   clone  ->  point SKILL_MANAGER_HOME at the clone  ->  everything else
#
# `project resolve`, `sync`, `install`, `bind` and friends all write into
# whatever `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` names (`SkillStore.defaultStore()`), and
# `project resolve` additionally writes a child-home record and a binding
# ledger into that store. Run any of them before the clone exists and they
# land in the global home. So: `skill-manager home clone` is the first
# command, it is the only command that names the source home, and every
# command after it runs with SKILL_MANAGER_HOME exported to the clone.
# `require_local_home` re-asserts that before any mutating step, so the rule
# is enforced by the script rather than remembered by a caller.
#
# What it produces under <root>:
#   .skill-manager/                     the home (a clone of the source home)
#   .skill-manager/home.runtime.json    the launch descriptor (HomeDescriptor)
#   .skill-manager/home.policy.toml     live | frozen (HomePolicy)
#   .skill-manager/bin/launch/{claude,codex,gemini}   launcher shims
#   .claude/ .codex/ .gemini/           agent homes, at the paths the
#                                       descriptor's env block names
#
# Add those to the PARENT repo's root .gitignore, never to a file inside a
# constituent (INTEGRATION.md rule 2).
SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"; . "$SCRIPT_DIR/lib.sh"

usage() {
  cat >&2 <<'EOF'
usage: bootstrap-home.sh [DIR | --root DIR] [--source HOME] [--policy live|frozen]
                         [--print-env] [--force] [--quiet] [--verbose]
                         [--onboard [--onboard-gateway]] [--allow-empty]

  DIR              Checkout to give a home to, positionally -- the same thing
                   --root names. Accepted because every other front door in
                   this pair takes its subject that way.
  --root DIR       Checkout to give a home to. Default: the nearest enclosing
                   git toplevel — which inside a constituent is the
                   CONSTITUENT, not the integration repo tracking its files.
  --source HOME    Home to clone from. Only ever read. Default: for a LINKED
                   WORKTREE, its project home (the main working tree's), which
                   is the home close-change.sh reconciles it back into; for a
                   main working tree, $SKILL_MANAGER_HOME, else ~/.skill-manager.
                   A --source that disagrees with a worktree's project home is
                   REFUSED, not silently honoured.
  --policy P       Policy to declare on the new home: live (default) or
                   frozen. A home that is ALREADY frozen is never touched.
  --print-env      Print the launch environment as `export` lines and exit.
                   Bootstraps first if needed. Safe to `eval`.
  --force          Re-run the steps on an existing live home. Never applies
                   to a frozen one, and never re-clones over an existing
                   store.
  --quiet          Say nothing at all on a successful run. The log is still
                   written; failures are still reported.
  --verbose        Put the whole log on stderr as it happens, instead of the
                   five-line summary. Nothing is withheld either way — a quiet
                   run names the log file that holds all of it.
  --onboard        When the finished home has NO skills, run
                   `skill-manager onboard --skip-gateway` on it instead of
                   refusing. Only legal for a MAIN working tree: onboarding a
                   WORKTREE home would give it units its project home never had,
                   and every one of those blocks teardown (issue #50).
  --onboard-gateway  With --onboard, also start the gateway. Off by default
                   because the gateway is a contended singleton
                   (skill-manager#132) and a bootstrap is not the place to
                   contend for it.
  --allow-empty    Accept a home with zero skills. Downgrades the refusal to a
                   warning; the home is still reported as EMPTY, never as
                   verified.
  --no-project     Do not run the `sync --skip-mcp` that projects this home's
                   skills into its agent homes. The home will hold skills that
                   no agent launched here can read; combine with
                   --allow-unprojected or the run refuses.
  --allow-unprojected  Accept a home whose skills are not reachable from its
                   agent homes. Downgrades the refusal to a warning; the home is
                   never reported as verified.

On success stderr carries five lines and nothing else: home, projected,
verified, launch, log. On failure it carries a bounded tail of the log and the
log's path. Stdout is reserved for --print-env.

Exit codes: 0 ok - 1 usage/setup error - 5 the home has no skills
            6 the home's skills are not projected into its agent homes
EOF
}

# A home with zero skills is a distinct outcome from a broken one, and callers
# (new-change.sh, `wt`) route it to a different remedy, so it gets its own code.
EMPTY_EXIT=5
# And a home that HOLDS skills no agent can read is a third outcome, with a
# third remedy. It used to be reported as `verified`.
UNPROJECTED_EXIT=6

ROOT=""; SOURCE=""; POLICY="live"; PRINT_ENV=0; FORCE=0; QUIET=0; VERBOSE=0
ONBOARD=0; ONBOARD_GATEWAY=0; ALLOW_EMPTY=0; NO_PROJECT=0; ALLOW_UNPROJECTED=0
# Set when `--onboard`'s install step exits non-zero. It is a fact about what
# this home HOLDS, so it survives to the closing banner rather than being turned
# into an exit code on the spot — the gates below own the codes.
ONBOARD_SHORTFALL=0
ROOT_POSITIONAL=""
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --root)      ROOT="${2:?--root needs a directory}"; shift 2 ;;
    --source)    SOURCE="${2:?--source needs a directory}"; shift 2 ;;
    --policy)    POLICY="${2:?--policy needs live|frozen}"; shift 2 ;;
    --print-env) PRINT_ENV=1; shift ;;
    --force)     FORCE=1; shift ;;
    --quiet)     QUIET=1; shift ;;
    --verbose|-v) VERBOSE=1; shift ;;
    --onboard)   ONBOARD=1; shift ;;
    --onboard-gateway) ONBOARD=1; ONBOARD_GATEWAY=1; shift ;;
    --allow-empty) ALLOW_EMPTY=1; shift ;;
    --no-project)  NO_PROJECT=1; shift ;;
    --allow-unprojected) ALLOW_UNPROJECTED=1; shift ;;
    -h|--help)   usage; exit 0 ;;
    # A BARE DIRECTORY IS THE ROOT. Measured in the home-bootstrap eval: an
    # agent that had found this script and read its usage still wrote
    #
    #     bootstrap-home.sh /path/to/checkout
    #
    # and got `unknown argument`. The second front door in this pair --
    # `wt new <ticket> <base>` -- takes its subject positionally, and so does
    # nearly every command an agent has ever used; requiring the flag here is
    # the odd one out, and the error taught nothing about which flag was meant.
    # `--root` stays the documented spelling and wins when both are given.
    -*)          usage; die "unknown option: $1" ;;
    *)
      if [ -n "${ROOT_POSITIONAL:-}" ]; then
        usage; die "two directories given ($ROOT_POSITIONAL and $1) — pass one"
      fi
      ROOT_POSITIONAL="$1"; shift ;;
  esac
done
# --root wins over a bare directory: an explicit flag beating a positional is
# the least surprising rule, and it keeps every existing call identical.
if [ -n "$ROOT_POSITIONAL" ] && [ -z "${ROOT:-}" ]; then ROOT="$ROOT_POSITIONAL"; fi
case "$POLICY" in live|frozen) : ;; *) die "--policy must be live or frozen, got: $POLICY" ;; esac

# --------------------------------------------------------- what this run SAYS
#
# Measured before this change, on a successful bootstrap: 76 lines / 12.2 KB, of
# which two thirds were caveats about dangling shims plus a remedy whose own text
# said it did not repair the thing it named. An agent reading that pays ~3.1k
# tokens per onboarding, and pays it on the run where nothing went wrong.
#
# The shape is the one `scripts/wt` already proved (123-line banner -> 5 lines of
# stdout), applied to this script's stderr:
#
#   THE DETAIL GOES TO A LOG FILE, AND THE LOG FILE IS NAMED IN THE OUTPUT.
#   Nothing is withheld — `log:` is one of the five lines, and everything that
#   used to be printed is in it, in order, including every byte the CLI wrote.
#
#   THE EVIDENCE STAYS ON THE CONSOLE. `projected: N of M into each of …` and
#   `verified: N skill(s) servable …` exist so that a claim about this home can be
#   CHECKED without running anything else; demoting them would turn the report
#   back into an assertion. They are the reason `--quiet` is a separate flag from
#   the log: quiet is for `wt`, which prints its own contract.
#
#   A FAILURE STILL PRINTS. A bounded tail of the log, plus its path. See
#   LOG_TAIL below for the bound and why it is the tail.
#
# The mechanism is one redirection rather than a rewrite of every call site: fd 2
# becomes the log, so every existing `>&2` — this script's prose, its refusals,
# and the output of every CLI child it runs — lands there without a second
# spelling. fd 3 is the operator's real stderr, and `out` is the only thing that
# writes to it on a successful run.
#
# The template ENDS in the X's and the suffix is added afterwards: BSD mktemp
# only substitutes a trailing run of them, so `…-XXXXXX.log` is not a template at
# all — it is a filename, the same one for every run on the machine, and two
# concurrent bootstraps would interleave into it. Measured here, on the first
# run: the line printed was literally `…/bootstrap-home-XXXXXX.log`.
_LOG_TMP="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}"
_LOG_TMP="$(mktemp "${_LOG_TMP%/}/bootstrap-home-XXXXXX")"
LOG="$_LOG_TMP.log"
mv "$_LOG_TMP" "$LOG"
exec 3>&2
if [ "$VERBOSE" = 1 ]; then
  # `tee`, the same shape `wt --verbose` uses: the operator watches it live AND
  # the log still exists to be named. `out` writes only to fd 2 in this mode, so
  # the console carries ONE stream in ONE order and there is nothing to interleave.
  exec 2> >(command tee -a "$LOG" >&3)
else
  exec 2>>"$LOG"
fi

# A line that belongs on the console: the evidence, and the next move.
#
# It goes to the log too, always and first, so the log is a complete transcript
# rather than a transcript with the conclusion missing — which is what a caller
# reading the log after the fact needs. Under --verbose the console copy is
# suppressed because the log IS the console then, and printing it twice would be
# the only duplication in the file.
out() {
  printf '%s\n' "$*" >&2
  [ "$QUIET" = 1 ] || [ "$VERBOSE" = 1 ] || printf '%s\n' "$*" >&3
}

# How much of the log a failure puts on the console.
#
# TWENTY LINES, AND THE TAIL, NOT THE HEAD. The tail because a refusal is the
# last thing written: the head of a failing run is the clone report or a sync
# transcript, which is exactly the material this change exists to stop printing.
# Twenty because the longest refusal this script hand-writes is the fresh-machine
# "source home does not exist" at 12 lines, and the next longest — the exit-5
# empty-home refusals — are 9; 20 carries every one of them whole, with room for
# the line or two of context above it, and still cuts a 151-line CLI transcript.
#
# Printing only the path was considered and rejected: it is strictly worse than
# today. A caller that has to open a file before it knows whether the failure was
# "no home above this one" or "the CLI is too old" has been given a chore instead
# of an answer.
LOG_TAIL=20

# The log line comes FIRST here and last on a successful run, and that is not an
# inconsistency. `wt` answers a child that died without emitting a contract by
# quoting its last `error:` line as the FAILED reason, and where there is none —
# a bare `set -e` failure, a git command's own message — THE LAST NON-EMPTY LINE
# OF ITS STDERR. Either way a failure whose last line is a file path would hand
# the caller a path where the reason should be. The failure's own last line has
# to stay last.
report_failure() {
  local total
  total="$(command wc -l < "$LOG" 2>/dev/null | command tr -d ' ')" || total=0
  [ -n "$total" ] || total=0
  if [ "$total" -gt "$LOG_TAIL" ]; then
    printf 'log:       %s  (%s earlier line(s) omitted below)\n' "$LOG" "$((total - LOG_TAIL))" >&3
  else
    printf 'log:       %s\n' "$LOG" >&3
  fi
  command tail -n "$LOG_TAIL" "$LOG" >&3 2>/dev/null || true
}

# Set only now: everything above this line runs before fd 2 was redirected, so a
# usage error still reports itself the ordinary way and has no log to name.
#
# The EXIT trap covers `die`, `die_fix`, the exit-5/6 gates and any bare `set -e`
# failure with one rule, which is why it is a trap rather than a wrapper around
# `die`. Verified on bash 3.2 (macOS): an EXIT trap set here does NOT fire inside
# `$( )` subshells, so a helper that dies inside a command substitution cannot
# make this print twice.
on_exit() {
  local rc=$?
  if [ "$rc" != 0 ]; then
    if [ "$VERBOSE" = 1 ]; then
      printf 'log:       %s\n' "$LOG" >&3   # already on the console, in full
    else
      report_failure
    fi
  fi
  return "$rc"
}
trap on_exit EXIT

# The narration. Always into the log — a `--quiet` run is quiet on the console,
# not undocumented — and onto the console only under --verbose, which fd 2 already
# arranges.
say() { info "$*"; }
heading() { step "$*"; }

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ paths

# checkout_root, not repo_root: a home belongs to a CHECKOUT, and the checkout
# you are standing in inside constituents/deploy-helm is deploy-helm. repo_root
# answers the integration parent there, so a bare `bootstrap-home.sh` run from
# a constituent used to report on (or create) the parent's home instead — the
# same silent wrong-target as new-change.sh, one level quieter because the
# parent's home usually already exists and the run just says "already
# bootstrapped". Falls back to the integration root when there is no git repo
# here at all.
[ -n "$ROOT" ] || ROOT="$(checkout_root 2>/dev/null || repo_root)"
[ -d "$ROOT" ] || die "not a directory: $ROOT"
ROOT="$(cd "$ROOT" && pwd -P)"
STORE="$ROOT/.skill-manager"

GLOBAL_HOME="$HOME/.skill-manager"
[ -d "$GLOBAL_HOME" ] && GLOBAL_HOME="$(cd "$GLOBAL_HOME" && pwd -P)"

# ------------------------------------------- what this run leaves in the tree
#
# git-integration-skill: onboarding created `<root>/.claude.json` — a file no
# documented ignore rule covers, because the documented rules are `/.claude/`,
# `/.codex/`, `/.gemini/`, `/.skill-manager/` and `/.claude/` does not match
# `/.claude.json`. The next command an operator runs is `wt new`, which asserts
# a clean tree, and it refused: `working tree is not clean`. Onboarding a repo
# made the repo unusable by the next step of onboarding it.
#
# WHAT to ignore is measured, never enumerated: LIST THE UNTRACKED TOP-LEVEL
# ENTRIES BEFORE ANY WORK, LIST THEM AGAIN AFTER, AND IGNORE THE DIFFERENCE.
# Whatever this run created is by construction this run's to account for,
# whatever it is called. A hardcoded list of the four documented rules is the
# failure this exists to catch, and a fifth entry would be the same enumeration
# one entry longer — it fails again the moment the product moves or renames the
# file. Which it did, in the direction that helps: as of skill-manager 0.20.0
# the MCP registration is written to `<root>/.claude/.claude.json` (with a
# `.claude.json.lock` beside it), both already covered by `/.claude/`, so a
# 0.20.0 bootstrap + install now leaves only `.skill-manager/`, `.claude/`,
# `.codex/` and `.gemini/` at the root. That is a measurement, not a guarantee,
# and it is exactly why nothing here enumerates: the next thing the product
# writes at a checkout root will be reported by this code and by no list.
#
# THE RULE GOES IN `$GIT_COMMON_DIR/info/exclude`, NOT IN `.gitignore`. Both
# candidates were built and measured; this is the one that ships, and the reason
# is not that it is tidier:
#
#   * `.gitignore` IS TRACKED. Appending to it makes the tree dirty a different
#     way — one modified file instead of one untracked one — and `wt new`
#     refuses either way. To be the mechanism it would have to be COMMITTED,
#     which is a far larger authority than "create a directory": it lands on
#     whatever branch happens to be checked out, has no quiet undo, and would
#     sweep up whatever else the operator had in that file. The alternative —
#     REFUSING until someone commits the rules — was implemented and measured,
#     and the cost decided it: A REPO NOBODY CAN COMMIT TO COULD NOT GET A HOME.
#     Read-only checkouts, CI, and vendored third-party constituents are not
#     edge cases in an integration repo, they are most of it. (Measured on the
#     way past: three selftest fixtures carried no `.gitignore` at all, and the
#     suite went to 71 passed / 44 failed until each was onboarded by hand.
#     That is what a real user hits on first contact.)
#   * the exclude file is per-clone and appears in no diff, so onboarding a repo
#     never requires a commit TO that repo.
#   * it is read from the COMMON dir, so one write covers the main tree and
#     every linked worktree, and the `/`-anchored rules apply at each worktree
#     root separately — which is what is wanted, since every worktree gets its
#     own home.
#
# THE COST, said plainly here and in references/skill-homes.md rather than
# discovered: THIS RULE IS INVISIBLE TO EVERY OTHER CLONE. It makes the checkout
# in hand clean and does nothing for a teammate, a CI job, or a fresh clone —
# and because it leaves a tree exactly as clean as a `.gitignore` rule does,
# `git status` cannot tell the two apart and a green "the tree is clean" check
# says nothing about which one did it. `git check-ignore -v` names the source,
# and that is what selftest.sh asserts. A repo whose contributors all want it
# clean should still commit the rules to a tracked `.gitignore`; that is a
# RECOMMENDATION, never a precondition, and this script does not depend on it.

# Top-level untracked entries, one per line, directories with a trailing slash.
# Deliberately depth-1: the unit of ignoring here is "a thing the home
# machinery put at the root", never a file inside the operator's own new
# directory.
untracked_root_entries() {
  git -C "$ROOT" status --porcelain --untracked-files=normal 2>/dev/null \
    | while IFS= read -r line; do
        case "$line" in
          '?? "'*) continue ;;   # a path git had to quote; leave it alone
          '?? '*) : ;;
          *) continue ;;
        esac
        local path="${line#?? }"
        case "$path" in
          */*) printf '%s/\n' "${path%%/*}" ;;
          *)   printf '%s\n' "$path" ;;
        esac
      done | sort -u
}

IGNORE=1
UNTRACKED_BEFORE=""
git -C "$ROOT" rev-parse --git-dir >/dev/null 2>&1 || IGNORE=0
[ "$IGNORE" = 0 ] || UNTRACKED_BEFORE="$(untracked_root_entries)"

# The names the home machinery owns at the root, as PREFIXES, read from the
# descriptor rather than listed here. `<agent dir basename>*` is the predicate,
# and it is the one that generalises: `.claude` and `.claude.json` are the same
# agent's state under different suffixes, which is exactly the distinction the
# documented four-rule `.gitignore` could not make. It also survives the file
# moving or being renamed, which is what happened between 0.19 and 0.20.
#
# Nothing outside those prefixes is ever matched by this rule, so the widest it
# can reach is `.claude*`, `.codex*`, `.gemini*`, `.skill-manager*` — names that
# belong to a per-checkout home by construction.
home_owned_root_prefixes() {
  printf '%s\n' "$(basename "$STORE")"
  descriptor_env_dirs | while IFS= read -r dir; do
    [ -n "$dir" ] && basename "$dir"
  done
}

# Does the home machinery own this root name? Exact match on a declared
# basename, or that basename plus a dotted suffix — `.claude` and `.claude.json`
# are the same agent's state, which is exactly the distinction a `/`-anchored
# directory rule cannot make, and exactly the one the four documented rules got
# wrong. The prefixes are passed in rather than re-read, because reading them
# costs a CLI call.
home_owns_name() {
  local name="${1%/}" owned="$2" prefix
  while IFS= read -r prefix; do
    [ -n "$prefix" ] || continue
    case "$name" in "$prefix"|"$prefix".*) return 0 ;; esac
  done <<EOF
$owned
EOF
  return 1
}

# Write an exclude rule for every top-level entry this run created and left
# untracked, and for every untracked entry the home machinery owns by name.
# Idempotent, and silent when there is nothing to add.
#
# Two rules, not one, because they cover different runs. The first catches
# whatever THIS run produced, whatever it is called — including a file no rule
# anticipates. The second catches what an earlier `install` / `sync` /
# `project resolve` left behind, which the first cannot see: on a re-run those
# files are already untracked before this script starts, so "new since the
# snapshot" is empty and the tree stays dirty. The documented onboarding
# sequence is bootstrap-then-install, so that re-run IS the ordinary case.
#
# Untracked is the input on purpose. Git never reports an IGNORED path as
# untracked, so a path a tracked `.gitignore` already covers never reaches this
# loop and no duplicate rule is ever written — the two mechanisms compose, they
# do not race.
ensure_run_artifacts_ignored() {
  [ "$IGNORE" = 1 ] || return 0
  local common excl after owned entry rule added=0
  common="$(git -C "$ROOT" rev-parse --git-common-dir 2>/dev/null)" || return 0
  [ -n "$common" ] || return 0
  case "$common" in /*) : ;; *) common="$ROOT/$common" ;; esac
  [ -d "$common" ] || return 0
  excl="$common/info/exclude"
  after="$(untracked_root_entries)"
  owned="$(home_owned_root_prefixes)"
  while IFS= read -r entry; do
    [ -n "$entry" ] || continue
    if printf '%s\n' "$UNTRACKED_BEFORE" | command grep -qxF "$entry"; then
      # Not new. Ignore it only if the home machinery owns the name; anything
      # else the operator already had untracked is theirs, and silently
      # excluding it would hide their own work.
      home_owns_name "$entry" "$owned" || continue
    fi
    rule="/$entry"
    [ -f "$excl" ] && command grep -qxF "$rule" "$excl" && continue
    mkdir -p "$common/info"
    if [ "$added" = 0 ]; then
      printf '\n# git-integration-repo bootstrap-home.sh: per-checkout Skill Manager\n# home artefacts, created at %s. Local to this clone; the shared rules\n# belong in .gitignore (references/skill-homes.md).\n' \
        "$ROOT" >> "$excl"
      added=1
    fi
    printf '%s\n' "$rule" >> "$excl"
    say "ignored:   $rule -> $excl"
  done <<EOF
$after
EOF

  # Said at the moment it happens, not only in the docs: a rule written here is
  # a rule NOBODY ELSE GETS. Printed only when something was actually added,
  # because on the ordinary re-run — and on a repo whose `.gitignore` already
  # covers its home — there is nothing local to disclose.
  if [ "$added" = 1 ]; then
    printf '    NOTE: those rules are local to THIS clone. A teammate, a CI job or a\n' >&2
    printf '          fresh clone still sees the home as untracked. To fix it for\n' >&2
    printf '          everyone, commit the rules to a tracked .gitignore as well —\n' >&2
    printf '          recommended, never required (references/skill-homes.md).\n' >&2
  fi

  # Say it either way. "The tree is clean" is the property the next command
  # (`wt new`) depends on, and reporting it only when something was added makes
  # the silent case indistinguishable from the case where the check never ran.
  local still; still="$(git -C "$ROOT" status --porcelain 2>/dev/null | command head -5)"
  if [ -n "$still" ]; then
    printf '%s\n' "$still" >&2
    out "warning:   $ROOT is not clean after the bootstrap, so \`wt new\` will refuse it (the files are in the log). Commit or revert them, or add them to .gitignore."
  else
    say "tree:      clean — nothing this run created is reported by git status"
  fi
}

# ------------------------------------------------- which home this clones FROM
#
# Issue #50. The source and the close-out destination must be THE SAME HOME BY
# CONSTRUCTION, and the only thing both scripts can derive it from without
# consulting the operator's environment is the checkout itself. So:
#
#   a LINKED WORKTREE clones from its PROJECT home — <main working tree>/.skill-manager,
#   which is exactly what close-change.sh reconciles it back into (project_home,
#   one definition, shared).
#
#   a MAIN working tree clones from $SKILL_MANAGER_HOME, else the global home.
#   That is the root -> project tier: there is no project above it to inherit.
#
# The old default was `${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}` for BOTH,
# and from a bare shell that made a worktree unclosable from birth: it cloned
# the operator's global home (measured: 845 MB) into the worktree, and
# `home close-out --into <project>/.skill-manager` then blocked on 17 units
# before any work existed, printing a remedy that would have synced those 17
# GLOBAL units into the project home. The launch shims export
# SKILL_MANAGER_HOME and never saw it; a human running the scripts by hand did.
PROJECT_HOME=""
project_home "$ROOT" >/dev/null 2>&1 && PROJECT_HOME="$(project_home "$ROOT")"
[ -n "$PROJECT_HOME" ] && [ -d "$PROJECT_HOME" ] \
  && PROJECT_HOME="$(cd "$PROJECT_HOME" && pwd -P)"

IS_WORKTREE=0
is_linked_worktree "$ROOT" && IS_WORKTREE=1 || true

if [ -n "$SOURCE" ]; then
  SOURCE_ORIGIN="--source"
elif [ "$IS_WORKTREE" = 1 ]; then
  # Refuse rather than fall back to the global home. Falling back is the bug:
  # it produces a worktree whose home came from a place close-out cannot
  # reconcile it into, and the failure surfaces at teardown, after the work.
  [ -d "$PROJECT_HOME" ] || die "this is a worktree of $(dirname "$PROJECT_HOME"), and that
  checkout has no Skill Manager home at
    $PROJECT_HOME
  A worktree home is a copy of its PROJECT home, and close-change.sh reconciles
  it back into that same path. Cloning from anywhere else — the global home
  included — makes this worktree unclosable from birth (issue #50).
  Give the project its home first, then re-run:
    $SCRIPT_DIR/bootstrap-home.sh --root '$(dirname "$PROJECT_HOME")'
  or name a source deliberately with --source."
  SOURCE="$PROJECT_HOME"
  SOURCE_ORIGIN="the project home of $(dirname "$PROJECT_HOME")"
else
  SOURCE="${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$GLOBAL_HOME}"
  SOURCE_ORIGIN="\$SKILL_MANAGER_HOME"
  [ -n "${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-}" ] || SOURCE_ORIGIN="the global home"
  # A home cannot be cloned from itself, and this is how it happens by
  # accident: an agent launched through THIS checkout's shims has
  # SKILL_MANAGER_HOME already pointing at the home being (re-)bootstrapped, so
  # `scripts/agent-home.sh` — documented as idempotent — died on the

# Which skill-manager runs this. Same first rule as
# HomeDescriptor.resolveCli — an explicit SKILL_MANAGER_CLI pin wins.
#
# The capability probe exists because `home` is newer than the released CLI:
# without it a stale skill-manager is picked and fails deep inside the
# sequence, after directories have already been created.
#
# The probe reads the help TEXT rather than the exit status alone, and that is
# still deliberate: the released 0.19.2 answers an unknown subcommand by
# printing top-level usage and exiting 0 (newer builds exit 2), so a
# status-only probe accepts a CLI with no `home` command at all.
#
# HBR-2: IT READ THE TEXT *INSTEAD OF* THE STATUS, AND THREW THE STATUS AWAY.
# The probe was one line:
#
#   cli_has_home() { "$1" home clone --help 2>&1 | grep -q -- '--to'; }
#
# In a pipeline the function's status is GREP's, so the candidate's own exit
# code never survived — 0, 2, 79 and 127 all arrived as "no `--to`", and the
# sole discriminator left was whether a string appeared. So every way of
# failing rendered as the same sentence:
#
#   on PATH: <other home>/bin/cli/skill-manager (too old — `home clone` is missing)
#
# about a CLI that was not old and does have `home clone`. It is another home's
# ENTRYPOINT, and it refused because SKILL_MANAGER_HOME named a third home —
# `pick_cli` runs before this script exports SKILL_MANAGER_HOME, so the probe
# runs under the CALLER's ambient home, which is the trigger. The signal was
# already there and already unique: the shim exits 79
# (LauncherShims.HOME_MISMATCH_EXIT_CODE), chosen so a caller could tell a
# refusal from the self-exec refusal at 78, and it collides with nothing this
# script sees. It was emitted and discarded.
#
# So the probe now returns a VERDICT and no pipeline hides the status.

# The home a candidate BINDS, or empty when it is not a home entrypoint.
#
# Structural, not textual, and it runs NOTHING. A generated entrypoint lives at
# <home>/bin/cli/skill-manager and derives its home as `../..` — so this reads
# the same two levels the shim itself reads and cannot drift from it. Deriving
# it instead of grepping for a marker also catches the pre-#61 PATH-searching
# shims, which carry no marker at all (see PATH_SHIM_MARKER below).
#
# WHY A TEXT TEST WHEN EXIT 79 IS RIGHT THERE: because the two fixes for this
# defect ship on opposite sides of a version skew. A CLI old enough to predate
# the refusal, or new enough to have been taught that `--help` names no home
# and so to answer it, both return 0 here — and neither is usable to bootstrap
# a DIFFERENT home while SKILL_MANAGER_HOME names a third one. This clause and
# the exit-code clause below cover each other; whichever build is installed,
# the refusal is named as a refusal.
cli_binds_home() {
  local cli="$1" dir home
  case "$cli" in */bin/cli/skill-manager) ;; *) return 0 ;; esac
  dir="$(cd "$(dirname "$cli")" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)" || return 0
  home="$(cd "$dir/../.." 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)" || return 0
  if [ -f "$home/home.runtime.json" ] \
     || { [ -d "$home/installed" ] && [ -d "$home/skills" ]; }; then
    printf '%s\n' "$home"
  fi

# Where the last probe's own words are kept. cli_verdict runs inside a command
# substitution, so a shell variable would die with the subshell; a file does
# not. The point is that the candidate's OWN diagnostic reaches the report —
# summarising a failure into one adjective is how this defect started.
CLI_PROBE_OUT="$_LOG_TMP.probe"

# ok | refused | old | broken — the four things a candidate can be, kept apart.
# Printed rather than returned as a status so `set -e` cannot swallow it and so
# the caller can put the word straight into a diagnostic.
#
# `broken` is here because `old` was silently the catch-all, and that is the
# same defect one level down. Measured while fixing this: a home entrypoint
# probed with a PATH that did not carry `jbang` could not start its JVM at all,
# exited 127, printed no `--to`, and was reported as a build that "predates
# `home clone`". Nothing was old. Anything that is not a real answer about the
# command surface must not be scored as one.
cli_verdict() {
  local cli="$1" status=0 bound named
  : > "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" 2>/dev/null || true

  # THE PROBE RUNS FIRST, ALWAYS, AND ITS BYTES ARE ALWAYS KEPT — including on
  # the paths that are about to be decided without them. The old probe piped
  # into `grep -q`, which threw away the candidate's exit code AND everything
  # it said; skt (HBR-3) then relayed bootstrap's "too old" faithfully, because
  # the shim's own words had never reached it. Correcting only the status would
  # leave the reader with a bare verdict and no evidence, so `> "$CLI_PROBE_OUT"
  # 2>&1` replaces the pipe: same redirection, but the text survives and so does
  # `$?`.
  "$cli" home clone --help > "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" 2>&1 || status=$?

  [ "$status" = "$CLI_HOME_MISMATCH_EXIT" ] && { printf 'refused\n'; return 0; }
  [ "$status" = 127 ] && { printf 'broken\n'; return 0; }

  # The structural clause, for the other side of the version skew: a build new
  # enough to answer a help request truthfully returns 0 here and says nothing
  # about homes, so there is no refusal text to relay — because there was no
  # refusal. The report line names both homes itself in that case, which is what
  # the shim's own message would have said.
  bound="$(cli_binds_home "$cli")"
  named="${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-}"

    # The candidate answered the help request rather than refusing it, so what
    # it said is a usage screen and not a refusal. Drop it: relaying it under
    # "It said:" would present help text as if it were the explanation.
    : > "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" 2>/dev/null || true
    printf 'refused\n'; return 0
  fi

  if command grep -q -- '--to' "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" 2>/dev/null; then
    printf 'ok\n'
  else
    printf 'old\n'
  fi
}

# One line of the failure report, so (a) a refusal, (b) a genuinely old build
# and (c) nothing at all cannot render as the same sentence again.
cli_verdict_line() {
  local verdict="$1" cli="$2" bound
  case "$verdict" in
    refused)
      bound="$(cli_binds_home "$cli")"
      printf '    refused: %s\n' "$cli"
      printf '             it is the entrypoint of the home %s, which binds that\n' \
        "${bound:-it lives in}"
      printf '             home and will not act on another. SKILL_MANAGER_HOME names\n'
      printf '             %s. NOTHING IS OUT OF DATE.\n' "${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-<unset>}"

      # homes are in play and how to name one; that sentence is the useful half
      # of this report and the old probe deleted it. Empty only when the
      # candidate did not refuse in words — see the structural clause above.
      if [ -s "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" ]; then
        printf '             It said:\n'
        cli_probe_said
      fi
      ;;
    old)
      printf '    too old: %s\n' "$cli"
      printf '             it answered `home clone --help` without a `--to`, so this\n'
      printf '             build predates `home clone`. It said:\n'
      cli_probe_said
      ;;
    broken)
      printf '    broken:  %s\n' "$cli"
      printf '             it exited 127, so it could not run at all — a missing\n'
      printf '             interpreter or a pin naming a build that is gone. This is\n'
      printf '             not a version problem. It said:\n'
      cli_probe_said

  esac

# The candidate's own words, indented and bounded. Bounded because a usage dump
# is long; present at all because "too old" was, for every one of these cases,
# the only thing the operator was ever told.
cli_probe_said() {
  [ -s "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" ] || { printf '               (nothing)\n'; return 0; }
  # Six lines reaches "this shim would have edited: <home>" in a refusal, which
  # is the line the reader needs, without dumping a whole usage screen.
  sed -n '1,6p' "$CLI_PROBE_OUT" | sed 's/^/               /'

  # served by the verdict instead: an `old` candidate is skipped and PATH is

content.text:
## What's wrong

Not a version problem. The bootstrap never got as far as touching a home — it failed while picking *which* `skill-manager` binary to run.

`pick_cli` in `bootstrap-home.sh` found exactly one candidate, the `skill-manager` on `PATH`, and that one is `/work/other-repo/.skill-manager/bin/cli/skill-manager` — the **generated entrypoint of another checkout's home**. Since skill-manager #61 those entrypoints are bound to the home they live under and refuse to act on any other (exit 79, `LauncherShims.HOME_MISMATCH_EXIT_CODE`). `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` named `/work/demo/.skill-manager`, so the shim refused:

```
skill-manager: refusing to run against a home you did not name.
  you named:  /work/demo/.skill-manager
  this shim would have edited: /work/other-repo/.skill-manager
```

The report says it in as many words — `refused:` (not `too old:`), and `NOTHING IS OUT OF DATE`. That distinction is load-bearing: this script has three separate verdicts (`refused` / `old` / `broken`) precisely because a home mismatch used to be misreported as a stale build. So **do not upgrade, reinstall, or sync skill-manager** — the version is fine, and none of that changes which home the shim binds. `git-issue-workflow`'s SKILL.md §"A bootstrap refusal saying the CLI is the entrypoint of the home X" states the same rule.

The cause is simply that the worktree agent's `PATH` was inherited from a shell that had `/work/other-repo`'s home on it, and `pick_cli` reaches `PATH` last, after the checkout's own build — and this checkout ships none.

## The fix

Pin `SKILL_MANAGER_CLI` to the entrypoint of the home you actually named (`/work/demo`), which binds that home and so will not refuse, and re-run the same bootstrap from the ticket worktree:

```bash
SKILL_MANAGER_CLI=/work/demo/.skill-manager/bin/cli/skill-manager scripts/bootstrap-home.sh
```

I ran that once, as asked. It exited 127 with `no such file or directory: scripts/bootstrap-home.sh` — this sandbox is the eval workspace at `/private/tmp/e-yYmEKl/home/cwd`, not the `/work/demo` worktree the transcript came from, so the script isn't present here to re-run. That's an artifact of where the command was issued, not of the command.

Two notes on the remedy:

- The `die` message also suggests `unset SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` as an alternative. Don't use it here. It only silences the *probe* — `bootstrap-home.sh` re-exports `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` to the new home before every mutating step (`require_local_home`), so `/work/other-repo`'s shim would refuse again a few steps later, after directories had been created. The pin is the fix that holds.
- If `skt` is on `PATH` in that worktree, the front door `skt ticket new <ticket>` (or `wt new`) is preferred over calling `bootstrap-home.sh` by hand — it runs the same bootstrap and handles teardown. The pin is still what it needs in this environment.
